standard.title: Develop inquiry questions
standard.description: develop questions for a geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge
standard.prior_knowledge: Students develop questions for geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge (AC9HG7S01). At Y7, questions were framed around water and liveability phenomena. At Y8, the same inquiry skill is applied to landforms and urbanisation contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop questions for a geographical inquiry related to a geomorphological or urbanisation phenomenon or challenge, including planning investigations at a range of scales.

nodes.label: What makes a geographic inquiry question
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristics of a productive geographical inquiry question — one that is investigable, geographically focused, and scale-appropriate.
nodes.minimum_width: Students can distinguish a productive geographical inquiry question from a too-broad or too-narrow one, explaining why.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain what makes a question suitable for geographical inquiry — investigable, addressing why a phenomenon exists or changes, and appropriate to the scale of the investigation — and apply this to Y8 phenomena (geomorphological processes, urbanisation challenges).
wider: Compare questions framed at different scales (local/national/global) and examine how scale changes what evidence is needed.
Examine how prior knowledge shapes inquiry framing — how does knowing about push-pull factors change the questions you can ask about urbanisation?
Develop a set of sub-questions from an overarching inquiry question, mapping the inquiry structure.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot generate or recognise investigable, geographically-anchored questions, the investigation they plan will be undirected — affecting evidence selection, data collection and conclusion quality throughout the inquiry cycle.

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit criteria for evaluating question quality before they generate their own. A framework (Is it investigable? Is it geographical? Is it appropriately scoped?) prevents vague or tautological inquiry questions.

success_criteria: Identifies and explains at least two characteristics of a productive geographical inquiry question.
Evaluates a given question against these characteristics, explaining whether it is suitable for geographical inquiry.

nodes.label: Planning an investigation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan a geographical investigation of a phenomenon or challenge, identifying appropriate scale(s) and investigative approaches using digital planning tools.
nodes.minimum_width: Students plan a simple investigation, identifying the question, at least one scale and one data collection approach.
nodes.typical_width: Students plan an investigation of a geographical phenomenon or challenge (e.g., how geomorphological processes produce significant landforms at local scale; causes and consequences of urbanisation at national scale), using digital planning tools and identifying the investigation's scope, scale(s) and methods.
wider: Develop an investigation plan that operates at two different scales, explaining how the scale shift changes the evidence needed.
Evaluate alternative inquiry approaches for the same question, explaining the trade-offs in data source selection.
Draft a preliminary inquiry hypothesis to guide the investigation.

response_modes.reason: Planning an investigation requires students to connect question development (Node 1) to method selection, scale identification and data source choices — integrating the inquiry design moves into a coherent plan.

success_criteria: Develops a geographical inquiry question and plans an investigation to address it, identifying scale and data approach.
Uses a digital planning tool to organise the investigation plan.
